details:
ZERO-G: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Project Overview

ZERO-G is an interactive 3D space-survival simulation game designed to help students understand the real-world challenges of establishing and maintaining a human outpost on the Moon or Mars. Players take on the role of mission commanders, responsible for building a sustainable outpost, managing limited resources, protecting their crew, and completing scientific objectives.

What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

Players begin by selecting a destination—either the Moon or Mars—and configuring their mission. They can construct and expand an outpost using different modules, including solar arrays, battery storage, life-support systems, water recyclers, greenhouses, radiation shields, habitats, science laboratories, communication relays, and emergency shelters.

Throughout the mission, players must manage essential resources such as power, oxygen, water, food, and crew health. Each mission cycle introduces challenges and environmental hazards. These include lunar dust, radiation, micrometeoroids, and long periods of darkness on the Moon, as well as Martian dust storms, extreme cold, and reduced solar power on Mars.

Players must evaluate different responses to these events and experience the consequences of their decisions. Science missions, an interactive astronaut companion, and mission reports make the experience more engaging and educational.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ZERO-G makes complex space exploration and engineering concepts easier to understand through interactive gameplay. Instead of simply reading about space missions, students actively experience the decisions and trade-offs involved in keeping an outpost operational.

The project aims to:

  • Encourage interest in STEM, particularly space science, engineering, and technology.
  • Develop critical thinking, problem-solving, and resource-management skills.
  • Introduce students to planetary environments and the challenges of human space exploration.
  • Demonstrate how engineering decisions affect crew safety and mission success.
  • Make scientific learning more accessible, interactive, and enjoyable for younger audiences.

Our intended impact is to inspire the next generation of space explorers, scientists, and engineers by turning space exploration concepts into an engaging learning experience.

Tools, Programming Languages, and Technologies

We developed ZERO-G using a frontend-focused technology stack:

  • JavaScript — Core programming language for game logic and interactions.
  • React — Component-based user interface development.
  • Vite — Development environment and build tooling.
  • Three.js — 3D graphics and environmental rendering.
  • React Three Fiber — Integration of Three.js with React.
  • Drei — Helpers and controls for the 3D environment.
  • Tailwind CSS — Responsive interface styling.
  • Framer Motion — UI animations and transitions.
  • Recharts — Resource and mission data visualization.
  • LocalStorage — Saving mission progress and player data.
  • Netlify — Deployment and hosting.

We also used NASA scientific resources and publicly available planetary data to guide the environmental conditions, hazards, and educational content represented in the simulation.

The project does not require specialized hardware. It is designed to run in a modern web browser on standard desktop and mobile devices.

What Makes ZERO-G Creative?

Our main creative approach was to transform a traditionally information-heavy STEM topic into a playable 3D simulation.

Rather than presenting students with a static educational website or dashboard, ZERO-G places them inside stylized lunar and Martian environments. Each planet has its own visual identity, environmental conditions, and survival challenges.

The game combines low-poly 3D environments, modular outpost construction, resource management, dynamic hazard events, science missions, and an interactive astronaut companion. Most importantly, the gameplay follows a Decision → Consequence → Learning approach: players make decisions, observe their effects, and learn why those decisions matter.

This combination of simulation, storytelling, exploration, and educational content makes the project an engaging way to learn about the challenges of living beyond Earth.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors while designing and developing ZERO-G:

  1. Scientific relevance: Planetary environments and hazards were informed by NASA resources and space-science references.
  2. Educational accessibility: Complex engineering concepts were simplified so younger students could understand them through gameplay.
  3. Realistic trade-offs: Resources are limited, and decisions can have positive or negative consequences for the mission.
  4. Planetary differences: The Moon and Mars have distinct environments and challenges rather than being simple visual variations.
  5. User experience: We prioritized intuitive controls, clear instructions, an interactive astronaut guide, and an accessible interface.
  6. Performance and compatibility: The 3D experience was designed with desktop and mobile usability in mind.
  7. Replayability: Different destinations, crew configurations, difficulty settings, and mission decisions encourage players to explore alternative strategies.

Ultimately, ZERO-G aims to make the challenges of humanity's future beyond Earth understandable, memorable, and exciting for the next generation.
